L303: Each admitted call carries the breaker generation it started in, so a slow result from before a newer opening cannot close or re-open the current breaker, and a cancelled half-open trial reopens with a fresh cooldown instead of stranding every later caller behind an abandoned permit. Each opening increments `agentops.circuit.opened_total`, so a breaker that flaps is visible in 【84†7.2. Monitoring】. Like every resilience seam, it only ever wraps idempotent reads — never a write.
L304: Keep the two disciplines apart when you design your own. A deadline, a retry, and a breaker decide how long you wait on a dependency. A guardrail decides what is allowed to happen at a trust boundary (【59†4.5. Guardrails】). Reliability failures cost you a turn; boundary failures cost you a state change.
L305: ## How are database rows trusted?
L306: SQLite is external input even when bundled with the repository. The data layer validates every row with Pydantic models configured to reject extra fields:
L307: 
L308:     `# simplified
L309:     class Incident(BaseModel):
L310:         """One incident parsed from the trusted dataset."""
L311: 
L312:         model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
L313: 
L314:         id: str = Field(pattern=_INCIDENT_ID.pattern)
L315:         service: str = Field(pattern=_SLUG.pattern)
L316:         title: str = Field(min_length=1)
L317:         severity: Severity
L318:         status: IncidentStatus
L319:         runbook: str = Field(pattern=_SLUG.pattern)
L320:         opened_at: str = Field(min_length=1)
L321:         resolved_at: str | None
L322:         summary: str = Field(min_length=1)
L323:     `
L324: `_INCIDENT_ID` and `_SLUG` are compiled once at the top of 【102†`models.py`†github.com】 and reused across models, tools, and normalization so a slug means the same thing everywhere. Schema constraints protect storage; domain models protect the Python boundary; tool validation protects model-controlled arguments. Each catches a different class of defect.
L325: Access discipline in 【103†`data.py`†github.com】 keeps those rows safe to reach. `_connect` opens writer-owned runtime connections with `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` and `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000` (a `PRAGMA` is a SQLite setting that applies to one connection). It then wraps any `sqlite3.Error` into a `DataAccessError` that names only the database file — never the query, so a failure cannot leak SQL:
L326: 
L327:     `# simplified
L328:     @contextmanager
L329:     def _connect() -> Iterator[sqlite3.Connection]:
L330:         """Open a constrained SQLite connection and wrap database errors with context."""
L331:         path = db_path()
L332:         connection = sqlite3.connect(path, timeout=5)
L333:         try:
L334:             connection.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
L335:             connection.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
L336:             connection.execute("PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000")
L337:             yield connection
L338:         except sqlite3.Error as error:
L339:             connection.rollback()
L340:             raise DataAccessError(f"SQLite operation failed for {path.name}") from error
L341:         finally:
L342:             connection.close()
L343:     `
L344: Readiness is a separate, read-only concern: `probe_runtime_database()` opens the state copy with `?mode=ro`, enables query-only mode, checks SQLite integrity, and confirms the required schema. Corrupt, legacy, or failed-migration state stays unready without the probe changing it.
L345: ## Why does the seed get copied?
L346: 
L347: Before runtime state exists, reads open `agents/data/incidents.db` with SQLite `mode=ro` and `query_only`; they never publish or migrate state. A2A startup or the first direct writer atomically copies the seed into `.state/incidents.db`. Later reads observe that runtime copy, still through a read-only connection.
L348: 
L349: This split keeps Git clean and lets every learner reset to the exact seed. `mise run data:reset` deletes `.state`, and the next writer copies the seed again.
L350: Publication is the interesting part: the copy is written to a temp file, `fsync`-ed to disk, and published with an exclusive hard link so a startup race cannot corrupt live state.
L351: Schema preparation has a narrower owner. A2A startup and each direct writer call `prepare_runtime_database()`, which locks only the runtime copy with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, adds safe audit columns, and creates the named idempotency index. It refuses duplicate keys with their exact invocation, action, and target before creating the index.
L352: Read tools and readiness probes never call that migration seam. A read-only MCP process observes the state that the writable A2A owner prepared; it does not change the database or the immutable seed.
L353: Deeper: why the copy is published with os.link
L354:

L356:     settings.state_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
L357:     temporary: Path | None = None
L358:     try:
L359:         # Publish a complete copy atomically. Two workers can race safely: the
L360:         # hard link is an exclusive create, so neither can overwrite live state.
L361:         with (
L362:             source.open("rb") as seed,
L363:             tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(
L364:                 dir=settings.state_dir,
L365:                 prefix=".incidents-",
L366:                 suffix=".tmp",
L367:                 delete=False,
L368:             ) as target,
L369:         ):
L370:             temporary = Path(target.name)
L371:             shutil.copyfileobj(seed, target)
L372:             target.flush()
L373:             os.fsync(target.fileno())

L377:         pass

L385: 
L386:     `flowchart TB
L387:         A[db_path called] --> B{.state/incidents.db exists?}
L388:         B -->|yes| R[return writable copy]
L389:         B -->|no| C[copy seed to .incidents-*.tmp]
L390:         C --> D[flush + os.fsync]
L391:         D --> E["os.link(tmp, destination)"]
L392:         E -->|link created| R
L393:         E -->|"FileExistsError: another worker won"| F[reuse the winner's copy]
L394:         F --> R
L395:         E -->|OSError| X[raise DataAccessError]
L396:         C -.->|always| U["finally: unlink tmp"]`
L397: `os.link` is the publish step precisely because it fails with `FileExistsError` if the destination already exists — that is an atomic "create-or-lose", where a rename could silently clobber a concurrent worker's live database. The loser's `FileExistsError` is swallowed (it just reuses the winner's copy), any real filesystem failure becomes a `DataAccessError`, and the temp file is always unlinked in `finally` so a failed copy is never published as valid state.
L398: ## How does a tool result reach the model?
L399: 
L400: A tool returns a plain dict, but that dict is not handed to the model as-is. `AgentOpsPolicyPlugin` registers `secure_tool_output` through its app-wide `after_tool_callback`, which ADK runs on every tool result from every agent. It treats each result — logs, runbook Markdown, MCP output — as attacker-influenceable data.
L401: With `AGENT_SANITIZE_TOOL_OUTPUT=true` (the default) it neutralizes known injection markers and 【104†spotlights】 free-text fields (`content`, `summary`, `lines`, `title`, `detail`, and peers). Spotlighting wraps them in `<<<TOOL_DATA data-not-instructions>>>` delimiters so the model reads them as data, not commands; identifiers, enums, and counts stay plain. It then always applies PII redaction before the dict re-enters the transcript.
L509: The same transaction records who approved (`approved_by`), why (`rationale`), and the current decision context reconstructed at execution (`context_summary`) — see the 【107†audit schema†github.com】.
L510: 
L511: The audit row proves what the action revalidated and recorded, not a frozen copy of what a particular UI rendered. The supplied client explicitly tells the approver to compare its arguments with the evidence immediately above.
L512: ## Why are mutation and audit one transaction?
L513: 
L514: `restart_service_with_audit` and `resolve_incident_with_audit` update state and insert the audit row on the same SQLite connection before committing. If audit insertion fails, the state change rolls back. A successful action without evidence is treated as failure.
L515: This is the tail of a single write's lifecycle — the confirmation, rationale, and transaction guards viewed as one state machine, where every terminal branch except one leaves state untouched:
L516: 
L517:     `stateDiagram-v2
L518:         [*] --> Proposed: agent gathers evidence, proposes the write
L519:         Proposed --> InputRequired: adk_request_confirmation
L520:         InputRequired --> Denied: human rejects
L521:         InputRequired --> Refused: confirmed, but no rationale
L522:         InputRequired --> Executing: confirmed, with rationale
L523:         Executing --> Committed: UPDATE + audit INSERT both succeed
L524:         Executing --> RolledBack: audit INSERT fails
L525:         Denied --> [*]: no state change
L526:         Refused --> [*]: no state change
L527:         Committed --> [*]: state and audit row persisted together
L528:         RolledBack --> [*]: state change reverted`
L529: `test_action_and_audit_roll_back_together` proves the `Executing → RolledBack` edge: a trigger that aborts the audit insert leaves the service still `down`. `test_action_rejects_a_missing_rationale` proves the `Refused` edge changes nothing.
L530: 
L531: The schema adds triggers that reject updates/deletes to existing audit rows. This makes the application log append-only, but SQLite on a writable volume is not a tamper-proof external audit system.
L532: ## Why not expose one generic database tool?
L533: 
L534: `query_database(sql: str)` would give the model far more authority than the task needs. It would also make policy and evaluation difficult: any prompt injection in a log line becomes an arbitrary query.
L535: Small, single-purpose functions create a capability allowlist — a fixed list of everything the agent may do. They also generate better schemas and produce meaningful audit and trajectory evidence: you can enumerate exactly what the agent can do and grade whether it did it.

L384: ## Which layers does another page own?
L385: 
L386: Two rows of the table above are taught next to the tools they guard, not here. 【101†3.1. Tools】 owns the guarded-write half of the pipeline: the `require_confirmation=True` pause and what a human must see before approving it, and why the mutation and its audit row commit or roll back as one transaction. A write's approval contract is part of the tool's design, so it is introduced where the tool is.
L387: Reliability lives with the tools too. Deadlines, bounded retries, and the opt-in circuit breaker decide how long you wait on a dependency; a guardrail decides what is allowed to happen at a trust boundary. 【102†3.1. Tools】 owns the first question.
L388: 
L389: What stays here is the policy that survives both: a write is never retried, and every write can be frozen at once.
L390: ## Why are write actions never retried?
L391: 
L392: Automatic retries are safe only when their whole failure boundary is understood. `restart_service` and `resolve_incident` change state, so only read tools get the resilience wrapper; guarded writes stay unwrapped behind human confirmation.
L393: Duplicate delivery is still possible after a client loses the response. Each approved write therefore persists `(invocation_id, action, target)` as its idempotency key. While holding `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, the data layer returns the first matching audit row before touching state, and a unique constraint rejects a second row. A replay returns the original evidence without applying the old mutation over newer state.
L394: ## How do you freeze every write for an incident?
L395: 
L396: Set `AGENT_WRITES_DISABLED=true` in the process environment, then restart the process or roll out that configuration. Every model-callable write handled by the restarted process refuses, with no code or image rebuild.
L397: Human confirmation gates each remediation action one decision at a time. Sometimes you need to stop all agent mutations together: a compromised session, a misbehaving prompt, or a change window you must not touch. When the kill-switch is set, `restart_service`, `resolve_incident`, and the unguarded `save_incident_note` memory write all refuse:
L398: 
L399:     `if settings.writes_disabled:
L400:         return _approval_error(f"restart of {name!r}", _WRITES_DISABLED_REASON)
L401:     `
L402: The refusal is deliberate in three ways:
L403: 
L404:   1. It short-circuits before any state read or memory database creation, so a frozen agent touches nothing.
L405:   2. It returns the same actionable `error` shape every other refusal uses, so the model reports "writes are frozen" instead of failing opaquely.
L406:   3. Reads keep working — including incident-note recall — so the on-call engineer can keep investigating while writes are frozen.
L407: `test_kill_switch_freezes_writes_before_approval` asserts an approved restart and resolve both refuse with the audit-log row count unchanged. `test_kill_switch_refuses_note_before_state_write` proves the memory database is not created. The out-of-band `forget_user_memory` operator command remains available for erasure requests; it is not an agent tool. Settings are read once at process startup, so an existing process does not hot-reload this flag.
L408: ## How do unexpected failures stay safe?
L409: 
L410: Model/tool error callbacks log the real exception for operators and return stable messages without raw provider, SQL, path, or secret detail to the model/client. Failures are surfaced, not swallowed.
L411: ## Can an optional managed service screen prompts for you?
L412: 
L413: Yes, for a fee, and you wire it in yourself. 【103†Model Armor†docs.cloud.google.com】 is a Google Cloud service that screens prompts and model responses for prompt injection and jailbreak attempts, responsible-AI categories (hate, harassment, sexually explicit, dangerous content, CSAM), sensitive data via Sensitive Data Protection, and malicious URLs.
L414: 
L415: Optional and proprietary
L416: This section is entirely optional and requires a Google Cloud project, billing, and the `modelarmor.googleapis.com` API. Model Armor is a proprietary hosted service, separate from the default Gemini inference path described in 【11†0.4. Providers】. Every core outcome — including every shipped guardrail on this page — is reachable without Model Armor. Skip it freely; read it to understand the trade.
L417: It complements rather than replaces what you built. Presidio redacts PII deterministically and locally; Model Armor adds a classifier for adversarial intent, which is the one category 【58†4.6. Security】 admits regex and allowlists handle poorly.
L418: Two honest caveats. First, it is probabilistic: a classifier that catches most injections is a risk reducer, not a boundary, and it must never become the reason a write is unguarded. The approval pause and the transaction above remain the actual control (【22†2.2. Models】 explains why the model can only ever ask). Second, it means sending prompt text to a third-party service — reconcile that with the data-protection posture the rest of this page defends before enabling it on real personal data.
L419: Deeper: what Model Armor adds, and how you would wire it
L420: Layer  | Catches  | Runs
L421: --- | --- | ---
L422: Typed validation  | Malformed arguments  | In-process, free, deterministic
L423: Presidio redaction  | Known PII patterns  | In-process, free, deterministic
L424: Model Armor  | Injection/jailbreak intent, RAI categories, malicious URLs  | Hosted call, paid, probabilistic
L425: Approval + transactions  | Everything the above miss  | In-process, free, deterministic
